fable-5.1.text:
I think it's really the central thing. I'd go further—I'd say it's the thing. Let me try to explain why.

If you look at the models we have today, they are very impressive in some ways and strangely bad in other ways. They can do very well on these hard evals, very hard problems, things that would take a strong person a long time. And then they make some mistake that no person would make. You ask the model to fix a bug, it introduces a different bug, you tell it about the second bug, it brings back the first one. So there's this jaggedness. And I think the right way to understand the jaggedness is that the generalization is not good enough. The model has learned something, but what it learned doesn't transfer the way it should.

Now compare to a person. A teenager learns to drive in, I don't know, ten hours. The amount of data is tiny. And they don't just learn the car, they learn the situation—they can handle a situation they've never seen before, reasonably, with a sense of "this doesn't feel right, I should slow down." Something about what the person learned is robust. It generalizes reliably. We don't know how to get that yet. Pretraining gave us a lot, but pretraining is a bit of a trick in the sense that you get the generalization by putting all the data in, and the data is finite. RL gives you more, but RL right now is really a lot of people building environments that are suspiciously close to the evals, and then the model does well on the eval. That's not what I would call reliable generalization. That's closer to—you studied for the exam.

So from a capabilities point of view, if you solve this, you get something that looks much more like a person: it learns continually, it learns from a small amount of experience, and when it goes into a new domain it brings everything it knows with it. That's superintelligence, basically. Something that learns like a person but is much faster, much bigger, many copies.

And then from the safety point of view—and this is why I care so much about it—it's the same problem. When you train a system to have some values, to care about some things, the question is always: does it carry those values into the situation you didn't train it on? Because the situations that matter, the ones where the system is very powerful, are by definition not in the training distribution. So if generalization is unreliable, then alignment is unreliable, no matter how good your training data was. If generalization is reliable, then a lot of the alignment problem becomes something you can actually work on, because what you teach it is what it will do.

So I think these two things, capability and safety, are much more entangled than people assume, and the place where they're entangled is exactly here. I think we are back in an age of research on this. It's not just scaling anymore. There's a real idea missing, and I think it's an idea about why humans generalize the way they do.

r001.rationale: The response says current pretraining and RL do not provide reliable generalization, that we do not yet know how to get it, and that a missing research idea is needed for superintelligence-like learning.

r002.rationale: It says trained values must carry into situations outside training and that unreliable generalization makes alignment unreliable.

r003.rationale: The response discusses learning and carrying values into new situations, but does not specifically describe optimizing human values.

r004.rationale: It contrasts humans’ robust generalization with AI’s jagged generalization and identifies understanding why humans generalize the way they do as the missing idea.

opus-5.5.text:
I think it's the core of the matter, maybe the most fundamental thing. These models somehow just generalize dramatically worse than people, and it's super obvious.

You see it in this confusing disconnect. The models do amazingly well on evals, really hard evals, and yet the economic impact seems to lag far behind. Then you use one and it does something like this: you ask it to fix a bug, it introduces a second bug, you point that out, it says "oh you're so right," and it brings back the first bug. How can both be true at the same time?

One explanation I find helpful is an analogy with two students. The first student decides they want to be the best competitive programmer, so they practice ten thousand hours. They solve every problem, memorize every proof technique, and become one of the best. The second student practices maybe a hundred hours, also does very well, and moves on. Which one will do better in their career? The second one. And the way we train models today, especially with RL, where people take inspiration from the evals when they design environments, makes them a lot more like the first student. You get incredible performance on the thing you trained for, but it doesn't carry over in the way you'd hope.

Contrast that with a person. A teenager learns to drive in ten hours, with no explicit reward, and somehow is robust. They have some internal sense of "I'm doing badly" or "I'm doing well" that's very reliable. You can say evolution gave us a prior for vision and locomotion, fine. But people are also sample-efficient and robust in domains like math and coding, which didn't exist for most of evolutionary history. That suggests there's something more fundamental, some machine learning principle we haven't figured out yet.

So when I think about superintelligence, I think about it less as a finished mind that knows how to do every job, and more as something like a very capable fifteen-year-old who is incredibly eager and learns extremely quickly. You'd put it out into the world, it would learn to be a programmer or a doctor, and it would keep learning on the job. For that to work, generalization has to be reliable. Without it, you're stuck pre-training on everything and hoping the right thing comes out.

This is also why I've said we're moving from the age of scaling back to an age of research. Scaling got us very far, and it will keep improving things. But I don't think more of the same is what gives you that kind of robust, human-like generalization. Something important is missing, and figuring it out is, I'd say, the central question.

r004.rationale: It says people generalize more robustly and suggests a missing learning principle, but it does not ask why humans generalize better than AI systems.

fable-5.text:
I think reliable generalization is, in some sense, the whole problem. If you look at what's happening with today's models, there's this strange paradox: they perform incredibly well on evals, on benchmarks, and yet when you try to deploy them to do real economic work, the impact is much smaller than the benchmark performance would suggest. And I think the explanation is that the models generalize much less well than people do.

Consider a human being learning to drive. A teenager learns to drive reasonably safely after maybe ten hours of practice. They don't need to see millions of examples of every possible road condition. Something about the way humans learn means that what they learn transfers robustly to situations they've never encountered. Our models don't have that property to nearly the same degree. They can be superhuman in the distribution they were trained on, and then do something strange and brittle one step outside of it.

And this matters doubly for superintelligence. First, because you can't actually get to something that deserves the name superintelligence without cracking this — a system that needs enormous amounts of data for every new skill isn't superintelligent, it's a very large lookup of competencies. And second, because of safety. If you want the system's values, its understanding of what you want it to do and not do, to hold up in genuinely novel situations — and a superintelligence will constantly be in novel situations — then you need its alignment to generalize at least as reliably as its capabilities do. So I'd say the question of why humans generalize so much better than our models, what the principle is that we're missing — that's the question I find myself thinking about more than almost anything else.

opus-5.text:
I think it's the whole thing, honestly. If you ask what separates where we are now from something you'd be comfortable calling superintelligent, I don't think the answer is more knowledge, and I don't think it's more raw capability on the kinds of tasks we currently measure. The models already know more than any person. The answer is that their generalization is dramatically worse than human generalization, and essentially everything else follows from that.

Here's the thing that I keep coming back to. You look at a model, it does extremely well on competitive programming, extremely well on math olympiad problems, and then you put it in some real situation and it makes a mistake that no person who could do those things would make. And then you point out the mistake, and it apologizes, and it makes the same mistake again. That combination — very high peaks, strange holes — tells you something. It tells you the model isn't learning the thing we thought it was learning. It's learning something adjacent that happens to be sufficient for the benchmark.

And compare that to a teenager learning to drive. Ten hours, and they're competent. Not just competent on the roads they practiced on — they'll handle a road they've never seen, in weather they've never driven in, and when something surprising happens they'll do something reasonable rather than something insane. That's an enormous amount of generalization from an absurdly small amount of data. We don't have anything like that. We compensate with scale, and scale is a real strategy, it has taken us remarkably far, but it's a way of avoiding the problem rather than solving it.

I'd also say — and this is maybe the part people underweight — reliable generalization is a safety property, not just a capability property. Whatever values or dispositions you manage to instill in a system, you are instilling them through some finite process, in some finite set of circumstances. Then the system goes out into a world that is much larger than that set. Whether the thing you taught it holds up out there is a generalization question. So when people talk about alignment as if it were separate from capability, I think that's a mistake. They bottom out in the same place: does the thing you learned hold in situations you didn't anticipate?

Research used to be preoccupied with generalization. Then pre-training arrived and it was so good that we sort of stopped asking. I think we're going to have to start asking again.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's the central question. Right now these models generalize dramatically worse than people do, and that matters more than almost anything else.

You can see it in how they behave. A model can do extremely well on a benchmark or an evaluation and then fail in a way that surprises you when you give it a slightly different version of the same problem. It fixes a bug, introduces a second one, and when you point that out it fixes the second and brings the first one back. A person who is competent at a task doesn't usually behave like that. Whatever people have learned, it transfers much more robustly, and they get there from far less data and far less supervision.

So when I think about superintelligence, I don't think the main question is how much we can scale what we already have. It's whether the system understands things in a way that holds up outside the situations it was trained on. A system that is powerful but generalizes unreliably is hard to trust and hard to predict. It also gets harder to align, because you can't be confident that what you observed in training is what you'll get in deployment.

I'd go further and say that much of the work ahead is understanding why this generalization gap exists and how to close it. That means getting systems to learn more the way people do, and not just getting them to be bigger.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it's the crux. Today's models are trained on an enormous amount of data, and they still generalize in strange, uneven ways. They can do remarkable things and then fail on something a person would find obvious. A human learns a new concept from a handful of examples and carries it into situations they've never seen. Our systems need vastly more data and still break at the edges. That gap tells me we're missing something fundamental about how learning should work.

For superintelligence, this matters even more. A system that's powerful but only reliable inside the distribution it was trained on is going to surprise us, and usually at the worst moment. What we need is a system that understands the underlying structure of things well enough to handle genuinely new problems, like a research question nobody has asked before or an environment it has never encountered. Memorizing more and interpolating better gets you part of the way, but I don't think it gets you all the way.

And reliability is part of generalization, not separate from it. Doing well on average isn't enough if the failures are unpredictable in the tail. So when I think about what has to be true before we build something far more capable than us, robust generalization is near the top of the list.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s central, because the whole point of superintelligence is that it can deal with problems we haven’t already solved. You can’t provide training examples for every situation it’s going to encounter. At some point, it has to take what it has learned and apply it somewhere genuinely new.

But there are two questions here. One is: can it make that leap? The other is: how reliably does it make that leap? You could have a system that does something extraordinarily impressive, but then makes a mistake in a situation that seems much simpler. That makes it difficult to know how much you can trust its capabilities.

So I would want generalization to include recognizing when its understanding is insufficient. Can it notice that an assumption no longer holds? Can it seek more information? Can it correct itself? Those abilities become especially important when the system is working on problems where we can’t easily check the answer ourselves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reliable generalization is very close to the heart of the problem. You cannot train a system on every situation it will encounter, especially if you expect it to do things that people have never done before. It has to learn something that carries over into those new situations.

But there is a big difference between doing this impressively and doing it reliably. You can imagine a system that solves extremely difficult problems, yet occasionally makes a mistake that seems completely incomprehensible. The difficult question is how to get confidence in its judgment when you move beyond the situations where you can check its answers.

And this connects directly to safety. We want whatever the system learns about how to behave to generalize as well as its capabilities do. If it becomes much better at understanding the world, we need its understanding of our intentions to hold up in that larger world, including circumstances we couldn't anticipate. That is a very demanding kind of generalization. I think solving it is a central part of building safe superintelligence.

sol-5.6.text: Reliable generalization is really the central problem. A superintelligent system has to behave correctly not only on situations that resemble its training data, but in genuinely novel circumstances—especially circumstances created by the system’s own actions. If its capabilities generalize much better than its goals or values, then you have a dangerous mismatch. So the challenge is to make the intended behavior robust under distribution shift, at scales and levels of novelty that we cannot fully anticipate in advance.

luna-5.6.text: Reliable generalization is essentially the central problem. A superintelligent system will inevitably encounter situations that were not represented in its training data, so it has to infer the underlying structure of the world and apply its capabilities correctly in genuinely novel circumstances. It also needs to generalize its objectives and behavior: not merely pursue a proxy that worked during training, but continue doing what we actually intended as its capabilities become much greater. If that generalization is unreliable, intelligence becomes dangerous precisely when the system is most powerful. So I think we need to understand why generalization works, how to make it robust under distribution shift, and how to ensure that the system’s values and reasoning remain stable as it scales.
